turns.t: I'm back about my heel, doctor. I'm a nurse, and the long shifts are killing my feet, so I'm hoping the treatment is working but it's not quite there.
Good to see you again. Let's review. How is the heel pain compared with last time?
A bit better, but the first steps in the morning are still awful.
How about by the end of a shift?
Throbbing along the bottom of the foot. By the evening I'm limping.
Any numbness, tingling or swelling?
No numbness, no tingling. No swelling that I've seen.
What have you been using since the last visit?
The ibuprofen gel, three times a day, and I've been doing the stretches.
Good. And the insoles I recommended?
I haven't got them yet. I didn't have the time. I'll order them.
Any other medical conditions?
Not much. I had a stress fracture in my foot when I was twenty. And my knees ache sometimes.
Any surgeries?
Only my appendix, years ago, when I was fourteen.
Let me check your pulse and temperature first. ~
Fine.
Pulse 70, temperature 36.6.
Great. ~
Please take off your shoe. I'm going to press along the heel. ~
Careful, it's sore.
There's tenderness at the inner part of the heel bone, and the arch looks quite flat.
So the stretches haven't fixed it? ~
They help, but it takes weeks. This remains plantar fasciitis.
How long will it take to go? ~
Often several months. Nobody wants to hear that, I know. ~
Not when I'm on my feet for twelve hours. ~
Please get supportive insoles, and wear cushioned shoes at work, and keep up the calf stretches before and after the shift.
Okay. I'll order the insoles tonight. ~
I'd also like to see you again in six weeks, and then talk about a steroid injection if it's still painful.
Six weeks. That's fine. ~
Make sure you rest your feet when you can, even for ten minutes. ~
I'll do my best. Thanks, doctor. ~
